newsitem.title: FRANCE: French study sees no danger from Cogema N-plant.
newsitem.headline: French study sees no danger from Cogema N-plant.

text.p: Government-appointed scientists said on Thursday they found no link between waste from a nuclear reprocessing centre at the northern French port of Cherbourg and a cluster of leukaemia cases in the area.

Charles Souleau, who led a scientific commission named by France's previous conservative government to study the dangers of radioactive waste from the state-run La Hague nuclear plant, told a public meeting that eating seafood and bathing in the area's waters presented no health danger.

The Environment and Health Ministry created Souleau's commission to evaluate a study by scientist Jean-Francois Viel who found the rate of leukaemia within 10 kms (six miles) of the plant to be three times higher than the national average.
But Souleau added that he had been unable to study all the details of Viel's report and would examine them more thoroughly in the future.
La Hague is owned by state nuclear company Cogema.
The Greenpeace environmental group said earlier this month it had found radioactivity levels exceeding European Union limits in waste spewing from a La Hague discharge pipe into the English Channel.
Cogema subsequently removed Greenpeace's equipment for analysing radioactivity levels. The environmental group is taking legal action against Cogema.
Viel, in a report published last January, identified 27 cases of leukemia diagnosed between 1978 and 1993 in patients under 25 years old and living within 35 km (20 miles) of La Hague.
